extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for composing and judging poetry, especially on imagery, diction, metre, characterisation, and the relation between intellectual depth and imaginative power. Draws contrasts between fifteenth/sixteenth-century practice and contemporary poets (Wordsworth and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery moulded to circumstance, passion, or character
rubrics_metrics.description: “As of higher worth, so doubtless still more characteristic of poetic genius does the imagery become, when it moulds and colours itself to the circumstances, passion, or character, present and foremost in the mind.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagery is most excellent when it grows from and reflects the immediate situation, emotion, or personality rather than being ornamental or detached. Examples cited: Shakespearean tragedy (LEAR, OTHELLO) and Sonnet 98 (spring imagery drawn from absent beloved). This is an evaluative mark of poetic genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery that unites succession with the feeling of simultaneousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagery should supply, with more than the power of the painter, the liveliest image of succession with the feeling of simultaneousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use swift, vivid figurative lines that convey movement and temporal compression (examples: lines about a lover breaking from embrace and gliding like a bright star). This quality produces vivid dramatic effect and is praised as a mark of high poetic imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and energy of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: “Depth, and energy of thought. No man was ever yet a great poet, without being at the same time a profound philosopher.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry requires intellectual substance — knowledge, reflection, and philosophical insight — not merely sensuous imagery. Creative power must be matched by intellectual energy; the best poems show wrestle and reconciliation between imagination and thought, producing sustained, not merely meteoric, poetic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery and dominion over language
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should possess “perfect dominion, often domination, over the whole world of language” — not be a passive vehicle of inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective poets study, meditate, and understand language so that knowledge becomes habitual and intuitive; the poet must actively shape language rather than passively transcribe impressions. This includes wide learning and the ability to assimilate and modify linguistic resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and individuality of images and characters (modern tendency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary poets more often propose new and striking images, rendering characters and descriptions specific and individual, even to a degree of portraiture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific, portrait-like detail can heighten interest and emotional engagement, but may be accompanied by sloppier diction or metre if not carefully handled. The criterion values striking, fresh imagery and distinct characterisation while recognizing trade-offs in diction and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exquisite polish of diction combined with perfect simplicity (older poets' virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: For fifteenth and sixteenth-century poets, excellence consisted in the exquisite polish of the diction, combined with perfect simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for refined, carefully chosen language that sounds appropriate in dignified conversation; avoid learned affectations and provincialisms. Arrange words melodiously so each part contributes to the harmony of the whole: subtle, restrained, and polished expression is prized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical variety by subtle balances in common metres (preferred over mechanical foreign metres)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater and more charming variety is produced by countless modifications and subtle balances of sound in the common metres of the country, rather than by adopting mechanical foreign metres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer nuanced modifications within native metrical practice to forced imported meters that carry an overpowering, mechanical tune (criticised example: borrowed Germanic metres). Aim for organic metrical variety achieved by sound balance, not by a single repetitive mechanical rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of the characteristic merits of both older and modern poets
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable poetic achievement would unite the high finish, appropriateness, delicate proportion, and pervasive grace of earlier masters with the keener interest, deeper pathos, manlier reflection, and fresher imagery of modern poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambition for poets: combine polish and melodic finish with vivid interest, emotional depth, and intellectual reflection. The passage urges synthesis rather than exclusive adherence to one period’s values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is essentially ideal and generic; avoids mere accident
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopts Aristotle’s principle: poetry, as poetry, is essentially ideal, it avoids and excludes all accident; apparent individualities must be representative of a class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters in poetry should exemplify generic class-attributes rather than being idiosyncratically accidental; the poet selects representative features that enable the universal or typical to emerge from particular details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude and representative quality in characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should possess verisimilitude and the representative quality that the purposes of poetry require — they must be persons of a known and abiding class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when characters seem drawn from a particular local life (e.g., shepherds), their traits should plausibly follow from conditions common to that class. Example: Michael is praised as an archetypal shepherd whose feelings and memories are shaped by his environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate selection of subject and milieu (limits of rustic life as poetic medium)
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of low and rustic life is only applicable to certain classes of poetry and is beneficial only when pre-existing education, sensibility, or reflective power is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rustic settings can supply concentrated elementary passions and memorable images, but without prior cultivation the mind may harden and become gross. Do not assume that rural life automatically yields superior poetic diction or thought; selection of subject must suit the poet’s purpose and capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against simply using 'real' conversational language as poetic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Wordsworth’s claim to 'adopt the very language of men': the essay objects that 'real' language is equivocal and that poetic diction cannot be simply the unedited language of rustic conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic diction requires selection, purification, and reconstruction: omissions and changes must be made to adapt casual speech for poetry. The best poetic language often derives from reflective, philosophic vocabulary rather than raw colloquial speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language formed by reflection on mental acts is the best part of language
rubrics_metrics.description: “The best part of human language, properly so called, is derived from reflection on the acts of the mind itself... formed by a voluntary appropriation of fixed symbols to internal acts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize concepts and phrasing that arise from intellectual reflection (moral/intellectual vocabulary), not only from immediate physical objects and daily experience. This supports the poem’s capacity to express general relations and laws, not just isolated facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame and manage speakers/narrators to avoid repellent realism
rubrics_metrics.description: When a poem adopts the voice of a dull or garrulous speaker (e.g., the narrator of THE THORN), an introductory framing-poem or adequate characterization is necessary; otherwise the imitation of dullness produces unpleasant sinkings from poetic height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a poet uses a deliberately unattractive or provincially realistic narrator, provide context or framing to prevent the reader from experiencing the speaker’s defects as the poet’s. Avoid uncounteracted repulsive details that distract from intended feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion amplifies but does not create vocabulary; poetic expression depends on prior lexical resources
rubrics_metrics.description: “The nature of a man’s words, where he is strongly affected by joy, grief, or anger, must necessarily depend on the number and quality of the general truths, conceptions and images... with which his mind had been previously stored. For the property of passion is not to create; but to set in increased activity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the poet has cultivated an adequate store of ideas, images, and words; intense feeling will magnify what is already present but cannot conjure new conceptual language out of nothing. Cultivate reading, thought, and reflective vocabulary to support passionate expression.
